text: Chapter 14 says three passes over an array are usually a cost worth paying. Worth paying for what, and when is that wrong?
choices: It is never wrong, since three passes and one pass are both linear.
For clarity, since each pass has one nameable job; it is wrong when measurement shows the traversal itself dominates.
For memory, since three passes need no intermediate storage while one pass does.
For correctness, since a single combined pass cannot maintain three invariants at once.
explanation: The last option is the trap, and it is nearly right. Chapter 32 confirms that both are O(n) — sequential work adds, and adding does not change the class — so asymptotically the decomposition is free. What it can cost is constant-factor and cache behaviour, which big-O cannot see, and the honest position is that the clarity is worth it until a measurement says otherwise.
